label: R8
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R8}
Let $u: E \to F$  
be a linear map between operator spaces  $E\subset A$ and $ F\subset   B$ 
with $A,B$ denoting  $C^*$-algebras as usual.
Given norms $\alpha,\beta$    on the algebraic tensor products $D \otimes_{alg} A$
and $D \otimes_{alg} B$,
assume that 
$\| Id_D \otimes u: (D \otimes_{alg} E, \|\ \|_{D \otimes_{\alpha}  A}   ) \to (D \otimes_{alg} F, \|\ \|_{D \otimes_{\beta}  B}   )  \|  <\infty.$
Then $Id_D \otimes u$ extends by density to a bounded linear map 
  from $\overline{D \otimes_{alg} E}^\alpha$ to $\overline{D \otimes_{alg} F}^\beta$.
  At the risk of abusing the notation we set
  $D \otimes_{\alpha} E=\overline{D \otimes_{alg} E}^\alpha$,   
 $D \otimes_{\beta} E=\overline{D \otimes_{alg} F}^\alpha$ and
 we still denote by $ Id_D \otimes u : D \otimes_{\alpha} E\to D \otimes_{\beta} F$ 
 the resulting map.
Then we may write
\begin{equation}\label{e8}\|u\|_{cb} = \sup\nolimits_{D} \| Id_D \otimes u: D \otimes_{\min} E\to D \otimes_{\min} F  \| ,\end{equation}
where the sup runs over all $C^*$-algebras $D$.
Moreover the sup is attained on the subcollection $\{M_n\mid n\ge 1\}$.
It is also attained on any large enough $D$ where large enough means that for any $n$
the identity of $M_n$ factors completely contractively through $D$. See e.g. \cite[p. 15]{157}.
In particular, this holds for
for $D=K(\ell_2)$   (the compact operators on $\ell_2$) or for $D=B(\ell_2)$, but also for  $D=\mathscr{C}$ which is    less standard,  whence
\begin{equation}\label{e7} \|u\|_{cb} = \| Id_\mathscr{C} \otimes u: \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\min} E\to \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\min} F  \| ,\end{equation}
which should be compared with our choice of notation 
\begin{equation}\label{e88} \|u\|_{mb} = \| Id_\mathscr{C} \otimes u: \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} E\to \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} F  \| ,\end{equation}
for which there is more to come.

title: Proposition

Consider  $C^*$-algebras $ A_j$, $  B_j$ ($j=1,2$) and maps
$u_j\in CP(A_j,B_j)$. Then $u_1 \otimes u_2$ extends to
a bounded c.p. map from $A_1\otimes_{\max} B_1$ to $A_2\otimes_{\max} B_2$ and
$$\|u_1 \otimes u_2 : A_1\otimes_{\max} B_1 \to A_2\otimes_{\max} B_2\|\le \|u_1  \| \|u_2\|.$$

because any separable $C^*$-algebra embeds in it as a $C^*$-subalgebra.
The analogous fundamental fact for our ``maximal" theory is that any separable unital $C^*$-algebra is a quotient of $\mathscr{C}$.

label: R1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R1}
In analogy with complete isometries, we say that a map
$u: E \to F$ is  
 maximally isometric or 
max-isometric 
if it is m.b. and the associated map $Id_\mathscr{C} \otimes u: \mathscr{C} \otimes_{max} E
\to C \otimes_{max} F$ is isometric.  In the $C^*$-framework of \cite{154},
such maps are called max-injective. \\ Obviously 
the restriction of a max-isometric map to a further subspace is still
max-isometric.\\
For instance   for any o.s.  $E$ the inclusion $E\subset A$ is max-isometric (this holds by the very definition of $\mathscr{C} \otimes_{max} E$). More significantly,  this holds whenever $E$ is an ideal. In particular the inclusion $A\to \hat A$ of $A$ into its unitization is  max-isometric.
Moreover, 
   if $A$ is a $C^*$-algebra the inclusion $A \subset A^{**}$
is max-isometric. See   \cite[\S 7.3]{154} for details on all this. \\
For an o.s. $E\subset A$, we   view 
$E^{**}$ as an o.s. using the natural embedding 
$E^{**}\subset A^{**}$, then the inclusion $i_E: E \to E^{**}$ is max-isometric. 
 
Also for unital $C^*$-algebras $A,B$ 
the maps $u_1: A\to A \otimes_{max} B$ (resp. $u_2: B\to A \otimes_{max} B$) defined by $u_1(a)=a \otimes 1$ (resp. $u_2(b)=1 \otimes b$) are 
 max-isometric. Thus for o.s. $E\subset A$ and $F\subset B$
 the same is true for the restrictions of   $u_1,u_2$ to $E$ and $F$.
head: environment
name: ``max-isometric"

title: Remark
body_md:
Consider a vector space $E$ given with two o.s. structures $E\subset A$ and $E\subset B$,  meaning two linear embeddings that represent it ``concretely".
Let $E_{\subset A}$ and $E_{\subset B}$ denote the corresponding structures.
The two structures are considered ``the same" if
$Id_E$ (the identity on $E$) defines a complete isometry
 from $E_{\subset A}$ to $E_{\subset B}$. 
 In that case the norms induced on $E\otimes_{alg} D$ by $E_{\subset A}\otimes_{\min} D$
 and $E_{\subset B}\otimes_{\min} D$ coincide for any $C^*$-algebra $D$,
 as well as the spaces $CB(E_{\subset A},F)$ and $CB(E_{\subset B},F)$, or
  $CB(F, E_{\subset A})$ and $CB(F, E_{\subset B})$ for any o.s. $F\subset C$.
In this framework, an ``abstract o.s."  is an equivalent class of o.s. up to
completely isometric isomorphism.
\\ In the new ``maximal viewpoint" that we are promoting in this paper, 
$E_{\subset A}$ and $E_{\subset B}$ will be considered ``the same"  if
$Id_E$ (the identity on $E$) defines a max-isometry
 from $E_{\subset A}$ to $E_{\subset B}$. 
  In that case the norms induced on $E\otimes_{alg} D$ by $E_{\subset A}\otimes_{\max} D$
 and $E_{\subset B}\otimes_{\max} D$ coincide for any $C^*$-algebra $D$,
 as well as the spaces $MB(E_{\subset A},F)$ and $MB(E_{\subset B},F)$, or
  $MB(F, E_{\subset A})$ and $MB(F, E_{\subset B})$ for any o.s. $F\subset C$.\\
  In other words, our maximal analogue of  abstract o.s.
  is   an equivalence class of  o.s. modulo maximally isometric isomorphism.
head: environment
name: ``maximal" analogue of an o.s. structure

title: Remark
body_md:
When $E\subset A$ and $F\subset B$ are $C^*$-{\it subalgebras} and $\pi: E \to F$ is a $*$-homomorphism, 
  clearly 
  $$\|\pi\|_{MB(E_{\subset E},F)}=1$$
  but it is not true in general that $\|\pi\|_{MB(E_{\subset A},F)}=1$, unless
  the inclusion $E\subset A$ is max-isometric.

label: R6
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R6}
Note that 
if there are maps $S_1 ,S_2\in CP(E,F)$ with $\|S_j\|\le 1$ ($j=1,2$) such that
$V\in CP(E,M_2 (F))$, then there are
{\it unital}   maps $S_1 ,S_2\in CP(E,F)$
with the same property.
   Indeed,
let $f$ be a state (meaning a positive linear form on $E$ such that $f(1)=1$).
Note  $0\le S_j(1)\le 1$.
Let
$$V_1(x)= \left(
\begin{matrix}
 S_1 (x)+f(x)(1-S_1(1)) & u(x)\\
 u(x^* )^* & S_2 (x) +f(x)(1-S_2(1))
\end{matrix}
\right).
$$
Then $V_1- V\in CP$  hence $V_1\in CP$ and  its diagonal entries are now unital.

label: nor
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{nor} Consider a linear map $u:E \to F$ between two operator systems
 $E\subset A$, $F\subset B$. If $u$ is positive then it is bounded
 (even if $E$ is non closed) with norm at most $2\|u(1)\|$.
 If $u$ is c.p. then $\|u\|=\|u(1)\|$.\\
  If $u(1)=1$ then $u$ is positive  if     $\|u\| =1$.\\
 If $u(1)=1$ then $u$ is c.p. if  and only if  $\|u\|_{cb}=1$.\\
 See \cite[chap. 2]{Pau} for detailed proofs.
head: environment

label: mpp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{mpp} Let  $u:E \to F$ be a linear map between   operator systems $E\subset A$ and $ F\subset   B$ 
with $A,B$ denoting  unital $C^*$-algebras.
The following are equivalent:
 \begin{itemize}
                  \item[{\rm (i)} ] 
 $u\in MP(E,F)$. 
 \item[{\rm (ii)} ] The maps
$u_D$ are positive for any $C^*$-algebra $D$. 
 \item[{\rm (iii)} ] The maps
$u_D$ are c.p. for any $C^*$-algebra $D$. 
 \item[{\rm (iv)} ]  The maps
$u_D$ are m.p. for any $C^*$-algebra $D$.
 \end{itemize}
In that case $\|u\|_{mb}=\|u(1)\|$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Consider operator systems $E_j\subset A_j$, $F_j\subset B_j$ ($j=1,2$).
    For any pair of  m.p. maps $u_j: E_j \to F_j$, the map $u_1\otimes u_2$
    extends to a map in $MP(E_1\otimes_{\max} E_2, F_1\otimes_{\max} F_2)$.

label: L1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{L1} Let  $A,B$ be $C^*$-algebras.
Any c.p. map $u: A\to B$ is m.b. with $\|  u \|_{mb}=\|u\|$, and $\|  u \|_{mb}=\|u(1)\|$  if    $A$ is unital. In particular $\|  u \|_{mb}=1$  for any u.c.p. map $u$.
More generally we have
$D(A,B)\subset MB(A,B)$
and  $$\forall u\in D(A,B) \quad \|  u \|_{mb}\le  \|  u \|_{dec}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows   from Haagerup's definition of the dec-norm
    once one recalls Proposition \ref{imp}.
head: environment

label: c1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{c1} In the preceding situation,  
$CP(A,B)= MP(A,B).$
head: environment

label: d1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d1}     For any map $u: E \to M$ from an operator space
 $E\subset A$ to a von Neumann algebra  $M$ we have
$$\|u\|_{mb} =\inf \{ \|\widetilde u: A \to M\|_{dec} \mid \ \widetilde u \in D(A,M),\ \ \widetilde u_{|E}= u\}, $$
and the infimum is attained.
In particular, $D(A,M)=MB(A,M)$ and $\|  u \|_{mb}=  \|  u \|_{dec}$ for all $u:A \to M$.\\
If $E$ is an operator system and $u\in MP(E,M)$ 
then we can find an extension $\widetilde u\in MP(A,M)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first part see \cite[p. 266]{P4} 
(and also in \cite[\S 6.3]{154}). 
Since $M$ is a dual we can use the weak* topology to show that the infimum is attained. Let $u\in MP(E,M)$. We will use Remark \ref{nor}. Let $E$ be an operator system. 
Assume  $u(1)=1$ and hence $\widetilde u(1)=1$ and   $\|u\|_{mb}=1$. If we choose
$\widetilde u$ such that $\|  \widetilde u \|_{mb}= 1$ and a fortiori $\|  \widetilde u \|_{cb}= 1$ then 
$\widetilde u : A \to M$ is c.p. and hence m.p. by the preceding corollary. 
This settles the unital case. For the non-unital case on $E$ unital, we will use a well known perturbation argument.
We fix $\varepsilon>0$ and we choose any state $f$ restricted to $E$. Let $u_\varepsilon(.)=u(.)+\varepsilon f(.) 1$. We define $v_\varepsilon\in MP( E , M)$ by $v_\varepsilon(.)=   u_\varepsilon(1)^{-1/2} u_\varepsilon(.)u_\varepsilon(1)^{-1/2}$. Since $v_\varepsilon$ is unital, by the unital case,  
it admits  an extension $\widetilde v_\varepsilon\in MP(A , M)$. Then, let $\widetilde {u_\varepsilon}: MP(A,M)$ be defined by
$\widetilde {u_\varepsilon}(.)=   u_\varepsilon(1)^{1/2} \widetilde v_\varepsilon(.)u_\varepsilon(1)^{1/2}$. We have
$\| { {\widetilde {u_\varepsilon}  }  } _{|E} -u\| \le \varepsilon$. Let $\widetilde u: A \to M$ be a pointwise
weak* limit of a suitable ultrafilter refining the net $({\widetilde {u_\varepsilon}  })$. The map
$\widetilde u\in MP( A , M)$ is the desired extension of $u$.
head: environment

label: d2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d2}  Assuming $E\subset A$ and $ F\subset   B$ as before, a map
$u: E \to F$ is m.b. if and only if
there is a decomposable map $\widetilde u : A \to B^{**}$ with  $\|\widetilde u \|_{dec}
=\| u \|_{mb}$
that extends the map $i_F u: E \to F^{**}$ 
where $i_F :F \to F^{**}$ is the canonical inclusion map, and
$F^{**}$ is viewed as a subspace of $B^{**}$.\\
The map $u: E \to F$ is m.p. if and only if there is a c.p.   map $\widetilde u : A \to B^{**}$
extending $i_F u$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the ``only if" part,  we simply apply the preceding statement to  $i_F u: E \to B^{**}$. For the ``if part" recall that $i_B: B \to B^{**}$ is a max-isometric $*$-homomorphism, and hence
$\|i_F u\|_{mb} =\|  u\|_{mb} $. Similarly, since 
$D \otimes_{max} B \subset D \otimes_{max} B^{**} $
 for any $C^*$-algebra $D$,
we have
obviously 
$(D \otimes_{max} B^{**})_+ \cap (D \otimes_{max} B ) =(D \otimes_{max} B )_+$
and hence 
using the notation \eqref{al}
$ (D \otimes_{alg} B^{**})^+_{\max} \cap (D \otimes_{alg} B)  =(D \otimes_{alg} B)^+_{\max}$ and therefore
$ (D \otimes_{alg} B^{**})^+_{\max} \cap (D \otimes_{alg} F)  =(D \otimes_{alg} F)^+_{\max}$.
\\
Thus  if $\widetilde u : A \to B^{**}$ is c.p.
it is m.p. by  Corollary \ref{c1} and its restriction to $E$ is m.p.
head: environment

label: R5-
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R5-} Let $u\in MB(E, F)$ for
operator systems $E\subset A$ and $ F\subset   B$. 
For any $C^*$-algebra $D$, 
let $u_D: D\otimes_{\max} E \to  D\otimes_{\max}  F$ be 
the map extending $Id_D \otimes u$.
By \eqref{e10'} we know that    $\|u_\mathscr{C}\|  \le 1$ (or equivalently $\|u\|_{mb} \le 1$)   if and only if  
$\|u_D \|\le 1$ for all $D$.\\
In analogy with the latter fact
we claim that  if $u_\mathscr{C}$ is positive then $u_D$ is positive  for all $D$, or equivalently $u$ is m.p.
by Proposition \ref{mpp}.\\
To check this claim it is easy to see that we may assume $D$ unital.
 Assume first that
  $u_\mathscr{C}$ is (well defined and)  c.p.
  Then the case when $u$ is also unital is easy using Remark \ref{nor} :   we have $\|u_\mathscr{C}\|_{cb}=1$
  and a fortiori $\|u_\mathscr{C}\| =1$. Now since $u_D$ is unital
     $\|u_D\|=1$  by   \eqref{e100}    and hence (again by Remark \ref{nor}) $u_D$ is    positive.
     This proves our claim when $u$ is unital.
       In the case when $u$ is  non-unital  
 we may argue as in the proof of Theorem \ref{d1}: without loss of generality we may  assume $F=B $, we introduce the unital map $v_\varepsilon: E \to B$. Our assumption that $u_\mathscr{C}$ is c.p. implies that  $[v_\varepsilon]_\mathscr{C}$ is c.p. The unital case tells
 us that  $[v_\varepsilon]_D$ is c.p. for any $D$.  Letting $\varepsilon\to 0$ we conclude
 that $ u_D$ is c.p. and hence  that $u$ is m.p. This completes the proof of the claim when we assume
 that $u_\mathscr{C}$ is   c.p.  Now assume $u_\mathscr{C}$  positive.
 Since $M_n(\mathscr{C})$ has the lifting property (see \S \ref{lift}) for any $n\ge 1$, we have a c.p. factorization of the identity of $M_n(\mathscr{C})$ through $\mathscr{C}$. It is easy to deduce from this  that $u_\mathscr{C}$ is   c.p.
head: environment

label: R5
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R5}
Let $E\subset A$ be an operator system, $C$ a $C^*$-algebra. 
While c.p. maps are m.p. when $E=A$, this is not valid
for maps defined on a general operator subsystem.  
Indeed, if $E\subset A $ is a $C^*$-subalgebra,
we may view it as an operator subsystem and then
the identity $u: E \to E$ is trivially c.p. but it is m.p.
only  if $u$ is m.b. and this means that the
max-norm induced on $\mathscr{C} \otimes  E$ by $\mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} A$
dominates the intrinsic max-norm of the $C^*$-tensor product
of $\mathscr{C}$ and $E$, which is not true in general, when the inclusion is not
max-isometric.
head: environment

label: mazur
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{mazur}
In several instances  when we need to  pass from the bidual $C^{**}$
to the space $C$  itself we invoke ``Mazur's theorem". By this we mean 
the famous theorem (a variant of Hahn-Banach)  by which for convex subsets 
of a Banach space $C$ the weak closure (meaning $\sigma(C,C^*)$)
and the norm closure coincide. We usually exploit the observation that
the topology $\sigma(C^{**},C^*)$ {\it coincides on $C$} with the weak topology.
head: environment

label: R15
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R15} Let 
$u: E \to B$ be a linear map from  an o.s.  $E\subset A$  to   a $C^*$-algebra $B$.
Since the inclusion map $i_B: B \to B^{**}$ is max-isometric (see Remark \ref{R1}),
$u\in MB(E,B) \Leftrightarrow i_Bu \in MB(E,B^{**})$ and
we have
 \begin{equation}\label{e40}
\|i_Bu\|_{mb} =\|u\|_{mb}.
\end{equation}
Note that this is not valid in general for dec in place of mb.
head: environment

label: d3
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d3}
Let $X\subset A$ be a separable o.s. and $C$ a $C^*$-algebra.  Assume that \eqref{e12} holds for any f.d. $E\subset X$.
Then for any $\varepsilon>0$, 
any $u: E \to C$ admits an extension $\widetilde u : X \to C$
with
$\|\widetilde u\|_{mb} \le (1+\varepsilon) \|u\|_{mb}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: See \cite[Th.3.5]{157}.
head: environment

label: d4
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d4} Let $E\subset A$ be a f.d. o.s. satisfying \eqref{e12}.
Then for any quotient $C/\mathcal{I}$ of $C$,
any $u\in MB(E,C/\mathcal{I})$ admits a lifting $\hat u\in MB(E,C)$ 
with $\|  \hat u\|_{mb}=\|  u\|_{mb}$. Here lifting means
that if $q: C \to C/\mathcal{I}$ denotes the quotient map we have $q\hat u=u$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
See \cite[Remark 4.2]{157}. The proof is the same as that of (iv) $\Rightarrow$ (i)
in \cite[Th. 2.6]{157}  applied to the class
 ${\mathcal{F}}$ equal to the class of maps with mb-norm $\le 1$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A unital $C^*$-algebra $A$ has the lifting property (LP)
if any u.c.p. map from $A$ to a quotient $u: A \to C/\mathcal{I}$ admits
a u.c.p. lifting 
$\hat u: A \to C$. If $A$ is not unital we say that it has the LP if its unitization does.  This is equivalent to
requiring that any completely contractive (in short c.c.) c.p. map
$u: A \to C/\mathcal{I}$
admits a c.c.c.p. lifting $\hat u: A \to C$.
head: environment

label: D1
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{D1} An o.s.   $X\subset A$ has the mb-lifting property (MLP)
if any mb map from $X$ to a quotient $u: X \to C/\mathcal{I}$ admits
a mb lifting $\hat u: X \to C$ with $\|\hat u\|_{mb}= \|u\|_{mb} $.
head: environment

label: arv
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{arv} By Arveson's principle from \cite{Arv}  (pointwise limits of liftables are liftables, see   \cite[\S 2]{157} for a more general formulation),
for the MLP with $X$ separable it suffices to check
 that for any $\varepsilon>0$ any $u: X \to C/\mathcal{I}$ admits
a  lifting $\hat u: X \to C$ with $\|\hat u\|_{mb}\le (1+\varepsilon) \|u\|_{mb} $.
head: environment

label: d6
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{d6} Let $X\subset A$ be a separable o.s.
The following are equivalent:
 \\
 {\rm (i)} The space $X$ has the MLP.\\
 {\rm(ii)} For any f.d. subspace $E\subset X$ and any $\varepsilon>0$  there is a subspace $\hat E \subset \mathscr{C}$
                                                         
                                          
such that $d_{mb}(E,\hat E)\le 1+\varepsilon$.\\
{\rm(ii)'} Same as (ii) with $\varepsilon=0$.\\
{\rm (iii)}  For any family $(D_i)$ of $C^*$-algebras, the canonical
(norm one) map $$\ell_\infty(\{D_i\}) \otimes_{\max} X\to \ell_\infty(\{D_i \otimes_{\max} X\}) $$
is isometric.
\\ 
 { \rm (iv)} Same as (iii) with $I=\mathbb{N}$ and $D_i=\mathscr{C}$ for all $i$. 
\\
 {\rm(v)} For any f.d. subspace $E\subset X$ and any $C^*$-algebra
$D$ the canonical isomorphism
$$ MB(E, D)^{**} \to MB(E, D^{**}) $$
is  isometric.
\\
{\rm(vi)} Any f.d. subspace $E\subset X$ has the MLP.
\\
Moreover, when $X=A$ (separable) these are equivalent to \\
 {\rm (i)'} The $C^*$-algebra $A$ has the LP.\\
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since the inclusion of $A$ in its unitization is max-isometric we may assume $A$ unital.
Since the proof is similar to that in \cite{157}
we only give a sketch.\\
(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) : we use $A=C^*(G)/ \mathcal{I}$ for some large enough free group $G$. Then we lift the restriction to $E$ of the map $u: X \to C^*(G)/ \mathcal{I}$.
This gives us $\hat u : E \to \hat E\subset C^*(G) $ with $\|\hat u\|_{mb} =1$
lifting $u_E$. Reducing the range of $\hat u$ we may assume that $\hat u$ 
is bijective, and then passing to a suitable countable free subgroup of $G$
we obtain  $\hat E\subset \mathscr{C}$ and the restriction of the quotient map
$C^*(G) \to C^*(G)/ \mathcal{I}$ gives us $(\hat u)^{-1}$ with $\|(\hat u)^{-1} \|_{mb} \le 1$, whence (ii)' and a fortiori (ii).\\
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) : By \cite{157} the algebra $\mathscr{C}$ satisfies (iii). Using (ii)
it is easy to check that any f.d. $E\subset X$ also satisfies  (iii). Equivalently
$X$   satisfies  (iii). \\
(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv) is obvious and (iv) $\Rightarrow$ (iii) follows from an elementary reduction to the separable case, together with the fact that any separable $D$ is a quotient of $\mathscr{C}$.\\
(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (v) is proved 
 using the description    of the unit ball of the dual of $MB(E,D)$ from \cite{157}.\\
 (v) $\Rightarrow$ (i) :
     Let $u: X \to C/\mathcal{I}$ as in Definition \ref{D1}. Theorem \ref{d4}  tells us that $u_{|E}: E \to  C/\mathcal{I}$ admits
     a lifting $v: E \to C$ with $\|v\|_{mb}=\|u_{|E}\|_{mb} \le \|u\|_{mb}$, then
     Theorem \ref{d3} tells us that $v$ admits an extension $\widetilde v: X \to C$ with
     $\|\widetilde v\|_{mb}\le (1+\varepsilon)\|v\|_{mb}$. Recall $q: C \to C/\mathcal{I}$ denotes the quotient map.
      Let $w^{E,\varepsilon}= (1+\varepsilon)^{-1}  q \widetilde v : X \to   C/\mathcal{I}$ (which is obviously liftable by $(1+\varepsilon)^{-1}    \widetilde v$). Note that $w^{E,\varepsilon}$ is equal to $(1+\varepsilon)^{-1} u$ on the subspace $E$.
      From this follows that $u$ is the pointwise limit
     of a net of maps indexed by $(E,\varepsilon)$ (namely the maps $w^{E,\varepsilon}$) that are all liftable by maps
     with mb-norms $\le \|u\|_{mb}$. By Arveson's principle (see Remark \ref{arv}), it follows that
     $u$ itself is liftable by a map
     with mb-norm $\le \|u\|_{mb}$, and we obtain (i).\\
          This gives us the equivalence of the five first assertions. From the equivalence
     of (i) and (ii) (or (v)) it is clear that (i) and (vi) are equivalent.
   \\  
     Lastly, if $X=A$ (separable) it is proved in \cite[Th.0.13]{157} that (iii)  is   equivalent to the LP of $A$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In analogy with (ii) a $C^*$-algebra $A$ has the LLP
  (meaning that $A\otimes_{\min} B(\ell_2)= A\otimes_{\max} B(\ell_2)$) if  and only if 
  for any f.d. $E\subset A$ and any $\varepsilon>0$ there is a subspace $\hat E \subset \mathscr{C}$ and a linear isomorphism $v: E \to \hat E$ such that  
$ \|v\|_{cb} \|v^{-1}\|_{mb}\le 1+\varepsilon  $ (note that here the two norms differ). Indeed, one way to check this
is to observe that $\mathscr{C}$ has the LLP and that using the above $v$'s one shows easily that
the LLP of $\mathscr{C}$ passes on to $A$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $  A$ be a separable $C^*$-algebra with LP. Then any subspace of $A$
 has the MLP. In particular, any subspace of $\mathscr{C}$ has the MLP.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
An operator space  $X\subset A$ has the OLP
if any c.b. map from $X$ to a quotient $u: X \to C/\mathcal{I}$ admits
a c.b. lifting 
$\hat u: X \to C$ with the same c.b. norm.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $X\subset \mathscr{C}$. 
                      Assume $CB(X, C) =MB(X,C)$ isometrically for any $C$.
                      Then $X$ has the OLP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since any  $X\subset \mathscr{C}$ has the MLP,
                      cb-maps from $X$ to quotients have cb-liftings
                      as required by the OLP.

title: Remark
body_md:
It seems open whether a non-separable $C^*$-algebra 
 with MLP has the LP.  Actually, it seems to be open whether
 $C^*(G)$
 has the LP when $G$ is an uncountable free (or even free abelian !) group.
 Nevertheless it is easy to check that the equivalence of (i)-(vi) in
Theorem \ref{d6} remains valid when $X$ is non-separable provided we replace (i) by 
the property that  
  every separable subspace of $X$ has the MLP.

label: ext1
title: Theorem

\label{ext1} Let $X\subset A$ be an o.s. and $M$ a von Neumann algebra .
Then any m.b. map $u: X \to M$ admits

label: ext2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{ext2} Let $E,X$ be   o.s. with $E\subset X\subset  A$  and let $C$ be a $C^*$-algebra.
Assume $\dim(E)<\infty$ and $X$ separable with the MLP.
Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$,   any m.b. map $u: E \to C$ extends to an  
 m.b. map $\widetilde u: X \to C$ with
\begin{equation}  \label{e11} \|\widetilde u\|_{mb} \le (1+\varepsilon) \|  u\|_{mb}  .\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By  (i) $\Rightarrow$ (v)  in Theorem \ref{d6}, Theorem \ref{ext2} is a reformulation of      Theorem \ref{d3}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Even if we assume $C$ with WEP, Theorem \ref{ext2} is  probably not valid  
if we drop the MLP assumption on $X$, but this is a somewhat {\it sticky point}.
Indeed,   
when $C$ has the WEP, the mb-norms of $C$-valued maps are the same as their cb-norms. So if  Theorem \ref{ext2} holds without the MLP assumption on $X$ for a $C^*$-algebra $C$
then the extension property expressed by \eqref{e11}
is valid with cb-norms instead of mb-norms and for $A=B(H)$.
In that case one says (following Effros-Haagerup)  that $C$ is ``approximately injective".
Kirchberg in \cite{Ki} claims that if  the WEP implies  approximately injective  then
  the WEP implies the LLP,   and the latter implication was disproved in \cite{JuP}.
However, as pointed out in the footnote of \cite[p. 362]{154} the argument for this claim is
unclear, and a convincing  proof that
WEP $\not\Rightarrow$ approximately injective  is still missing.

label: L6
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{L6} Let $E\subset A$ be a f.d. operator system, $C$ a unital $C^*$-algebra.
Assume that the $C^*$-algebra $A$ has the MLP.
For any m.p. map $u: E \to C^{**}$ with $\|u\|\le 1$ such that $u(1)\in C$,
there is a net of m.p. maps
$u_i: E \to C $ with $\|u_i\|\le 1$ tending pointwise
weak* to $u$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For unital maps this is Corollary 3.9. in \cite{157}.
The case when $u(1)\in C$ follows by a well known trick.
Let $\varepsilon>0$ and let $f$ be a state on $E$. Let
$u_\varepsilon(.)= u(.)+ \varepsilon f(.) 1$. Note
$u_\varepsilon(1)\in C$ and is invertible. Let
$v_\varepsilon(.)= u_\varepsilon(1)^{-1/2} u_\varepsilon(.) u_\varepsilon(1)^{-1/2}$ so that $v_\varepsilon(1)=1$.
Applying the unital case,
we have a net $v_i$ of $C$-valued unital m.p. maps tending pointwise
weak* to $v_\varepsilon$. Then
$u_i(.)=u_\varepsilon(1)^{1/2} v_i(.) u_\varepsilon(1)^{1/2}$ tends weak* to $u_\varepsilon$.
Since $\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\|u-u_\varepsilon\|=0$ the announced result follows.
head: environment

label: T1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T1} Let  $  A,C $ be  $C^*$-algebras. Assume $A$ has the MLP and let $E\subset A$ be a f.d. 
operator system.
Let $u: E \to C$. The following are equivalent.
  \item{(i)} We have $\|u\|_{mb} \le 1$.
    \item{(ii)} For any f.d. operator system $E_1$ with $E\subset E_1 \subset A$ and any $\varepsilon>0$
    there is a map $  u_1: E_1 \to C$ extending $u$ and such that $\|u_1\|_{dec} <1+\varepsilon$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume (i). By Theorem \ref{d2}  (note $E_1$ has the MLP) there is 
$v: E_1 \to C^{**}$ extending $i_C u$ such that $\|v\|_{dec}\le \|v\|_{mb}\le 1$.
Whence  $C^{**}$-valued {\it unital} c.p. maps 
$S_1,S_2$
such that
$V: x\mapsto \left(\begin{matrix}
 S_1 (x) &  v(x)\\
 v(x^* )^* & S_2 (x)
\end{matrix}\right)$
is in $CP(E_1, C^{**})$ (see Remark \ref{R6}). Note 
$v(1)\in C$   since $v_{|E}=u$ and hence $V(1)\in M_2(C)$.
By Lemma \ref{L6} there is a net of m.p. maps $V_i: E_1\to M_2(C)$
with $\|V_i\|\le 1$ tending pointwise weak* to $V$.
In particular $(V_i)_{12} $ restricted to $E$ tends pointwise weak* to $ u$.
Passing to suitable convex hulls and using Mazur's theorem
we can find (possibly different) c.p. maps $V_i$ with $\|V_i\|\le 1$  for which
$(V_i)_{12} $ restricted to $E$ tends pointwise in norm to $ u$.
Choose then $i$ so that $\|  u - {(V_i)_{12}}_{|E} \|  <\varepsilon$.
Let then $v'=  (V_i)_{12} :E_1 \to C$. We have $\|v'_{|E}-u\|< \varepsilon$
  and 
$\|v'\|_{dec} \le 1 $ (since $\|V_i\|\le 1$). By the elementary perturbation argument
described in \cite[Rem. 3.4]{157} there is a map $v'': E_1\to C$ such that
$v''_{|E}=u$ with $\|v''\|_{dec} \le 1+f(\varepsilon)$ where $f(\varepsilon)\to 0$ when $\varepsilon\to 0$. 
Thus we obtain (ii).\\
 Assume (ii). By a simple ultraproduct argument involving the net of maps
 $  u_1: E_1 \to C$ (indexed by f.d. subspaces $E_1$ with $E\subset E_1 \subset X$ and $\varepsilon>0$)
 we obtain a map $\widetilde u: A \to C^{**} $ with $\|\widetilde u\|_{dec} \le 1$
 extending $i_C u: E \to C^{**} $. Equivalently $\|\widetilde u\|_{mb} \le 1$ (see Theorem \ref{d1})
 and a fortiori $\|  i_C u \|_{mb}= \|\widetilde u_{|E}\|_{mb} \le 1$. By \eqref{e40} $\|    u \|_{mb}\le 1$.

label: wep
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{wep} The following properties of a $C^*$-algebra  $C$ are equivalent.\\
{\rm (i)}  $C$ has the WEP.\\
{\rm (ii)} For any $C^*$-algebra $A$ and any o.s. $E\subset A$  we have
$CB(E,C)=MB(E,C)$   isometrically.\\
{\rm (iii)} For any pair $E ,F$ of f.d. o.s. with $E \subset F\subset \mathscr{C}$, any $\varepsilon>0$ and
 any $u\in CB(E,C)$    there is   $\widetilde u: F \to C^{**}$ with 
$\|\widetilde u\|_{mb} \le (1+\varepsilon)  \|  u\|_{cb}$ such that ${\widetilde u}_{|E}=i_C u$.\\
{\rm (iv)} For any pair $E ,F$ of f.d. o.s. with $E \subset F\subset \mathscr{C}$, any $\varepsilon>0$ and
 any $u\in CB(E,C)$    there is   $\widetilde u: F \to C $ with 
$\|\widetilde u\|_{cb} \le (1+\varepsilon)  \|  u\|_{cb}$ such that ${\widetilde u}_{|E}=  u$.\\
{\rm (v)} For any f.d. $E\subset \mathscr{C}$ and any $\varepsilon>0$, any c.b. $u: E \to C$ admits an extension
$\widetilde u: \mathscr{C} \to C$ with $\|\widetilde u\|_{cb} \le  (1+\varepsilon)  \|  u\|_{cb}$.\\
{\rm (vi)} Same as (iv) with $F$ restricted to be a subspace spanned by  a finite number of the free unitary generators of $\mathscr{C}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first give the simple  proof that (i) $\Leftrightarrow$ (ii), then   outline the proof of 
 the other equivalences.\\
(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) is obvious as we just observed. 
Conversely, if (ii) holds, we have $\|u\|_{mb}=\|u\|_{cb}$ for any $u: E \to C$. Assuming $C\subset B(H)$ we may apply this with
$E=C$,  $A=B(H)$, and $u(x)=x$ for $x\in E$. Then  $\|u\|_{mb}=\|u\|_{cb}=1$ tells us that 
the max-norm on $\mathscr{C} \otimes C$ is $\le $ the norm induced on it by the max-norm
on $\mathscr{C} \otimes B(H)$, which is equal to the min-norm by Kirchberg's theorem.
So the latter induced norm on $\mathscr{C} \otimes C$ is also the min-norm.  It follows that
the max-norm and the min-norm are identical on $\mathscr{C}\otimes C$.
Equivalently $C$ has the WEP, proving  (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i). \\
Assume (ii). By Theorem \ref{ext1} any $u\in CB(E,C)=MB(E,C)$ admits an ``extension"
$\widetilde u\in MB(F,C^{**})$ with $  \|\widetilde u\|_{mb} \le (1+\varepsilon)  \|  u\|_{cb}$,
whence (iii). Assume (iii). 
By   Theorem \ref{d6}, there is a net $(\widetilde u_i)$
in the ball of radius $1+\varepsilon$ in  $MB(F,C )$ tending
pointwise weak* to $\widetilde u$. A fortiori $\|\widetilde u_i\|_{cb} \le 1+\varepsilon$.
Passing to convex combinations using Mazur's theorem
one gets a net $(u_i)$ in the same cb-ball such that the restrictions $({u_i}_{|E})$
converge pointwise in norm to $u$. Then a perturbation argument (as in the proof of Theorem \ref{T1})  leads to (iv). Assume (iv). Fix a f.d. $E\subset \mathscr{C}$ and  $u\in CB(E,C)$. 
Let $E=E_0 \subset \cdots E_n\subset E_{n+1}\subset \cdots  \subset \mathscr{C}$ be a sequence of f.d. subspaces with dense union $V=\cup E_n$. Let $\varepsilon_n>0$
be such that $\prod (1+\varepsilon_n) <1+\varepsilon$. By applying (iv)  to each $E_n$ we find
a map $\widetilde u: V \to C$ with $\|\widetilde u\|_{cb} \le 1+\varepsilon$ extending $u$.
We may then extend $\widetilde u$ to the whole of $\mathscr{C}$ by density of $V$,
whence (v). Clearly (v) implies (iv) which implies (vi).
By \cite[Th. 21.3]{157} 
 (vi) and (i) are equivalent.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $X\subset A$ be a subspace of a $C^*$-algebra $A$, with
                     dual $X^*$ as above.
                     There is a (completely) isometric embeddding $X^*\subset L$ in a $C^*$-algebra $L=L_{X\subset A}$ (of the form $\ell_\infty(I,\mathscr{C})$ for some suitably large index set $I$) such that for any $s\in  \mathscr{C} \otimes_{alg} X^*  $ with associated linear map 
                     $u_s : X \to \mathscr{C}$ we have
                     $$ \|s\|_{\max}=\|u_s\|_{mb} ,$$
                     and hence for any $Y\subset \mathscr{C}$  we have an isometric identity
                      $$Y \otimes_{\max} X^* =\overline{F(X,Y)}^{mb} \subset MB(X,Y).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $I$ denote the unit ball of $\mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} X$.
                       Any $t\in I$ defines a linear map $v_t: X^* \to \mathscr{C}$.
                       Let $j: X^* \to \ell_\infty(I,\mathscr{C})$ be the map taking
                       $\xi \in X^*$ to $(v_t(\xi))_{t\in I} $. Since $\|v_t\|_{cb} =\|t\|_{\min} \le \|t\|_{\max} \le 1$ we have $\|j\|_{cb}\le 1$. 
                       Moreover since
                       $M_n$ has the MLP (and is a quotient of $\mathscr{C}$), there is a max-isometric imbedding $M_n\subset \mathscr{C}$   for any $n$, so we may use the $v_t$'s with range in such copies of $M_n$ to show that
                         the map $j$
                       is completely isometric on the dual $X^*$
                       (in the o.s. sense) of $X$.\\
                       Let $s\in  \mathscr{C} \otimes_{alg} X^*$.
                       Then since $\mathscr{C}$ has the LP we know
                       that $\mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} \ell_\infty(I,\mathscr{C}) \subset 
                       \ell_\infty(I, \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} \mathscr{C})$ isometrically
                       (see (iii) in Th. \ref{d3}) and hence
                       $$\|s\|_{\max} = \sup_{t\in I} \|[Id \otimes v_t](s) \|_{\max}= \sup_{t\in I}\|[Id \otimes u_s](t) \|_{\max}
                        $$
                       where for the last equality we used the
                      fact that  $[Id \otimes v_t](s)$ and $[Id \otimes u_s](t)$ coincide
                      after flipping the factors.
                       Whence  $ \|s\|_{\max}=\|u_s\|_{mb} $. Since (by definition)
                       $Y \otimes_{\max} X^* \subset \mathscr{C} \otimes_{\max} X^*$
                       the rest is clear.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $X\subset A $ and $Y\subset B$ be o.s.
with duals $X^*\subset L_{X\subset A}$  and $Y^*\subset L_{Y\subset B}$
as above. 
For any $u\in MB(X,Y)$, we have $\|u^*: Y^* \to X^*\|_{mb} \le \|u\|_{mb}$.
Indeed, this boils down to the fact that
for any $w: Y \to \mathscr{C}$ of finite rank we have $\|wu\|_{mb} \le \|w\|_{mb} \|u\|_{mb}$.\\
More precisely, 
let  $R(u): MB(Y,\mathscr{C}) \to MB(X,\mathscr{C})$ be defined by $R(u)(v)=vu$.
Then $$\|u^*: Y^* \to X^*\|_{mb}=\|R(u):MB_0(Y,\mathscr{C}) \to MB_0(X,\mathscr{C})\|,$$
where $MB_0(X,\mathscr{C})$ denotes the closure in $MB(X,\mathscr{C})$ of the set of finite rank
maps.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In Kirchberg's reformulation, the Connes embedding problem
asks whether the min and max norms are equivalent
on $\mathscr{C} \otimes \mathscr{C}$. If it was the case then,
for any $L= \ell_\infty(I,\mathscr{C}) $,  the max norm on $L\otimes \mathscr{C}$
would be also equal to the min norm, so that 
we would have always $X^*\otimes_{\max} \mathscr{C}= X^*\otimes_{\min} \mathscr{C}$, and hence the ``dual" embeddings $X^*\subset L_{X\subset A}$ 
 and $Y^*\subset L_{Y\subset D}$ would give us
 $\|u^*: Y^* \to X^*\|_{mb}= \|u^*: Y^* \to X^*\|_{cb}$.

label: pp1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pp1}  A multiplier  $M_\varphi: \mathbb{C}[G] \to \mathbb{C}[G]$ 
                     is m.b.
                  on $C^*_\lambda(G)$ if and only if  the function $\varphi: G \to \mathbb{C}$
               is in the space $B(G)$
               and $\|M_\varphi: C^*_\lambda(G) \to C^*_\lambda(G)\|_{mb}=\|\varphi\|_{B(G)}$.
head: environment

label: Tmul
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Tmul}  The following properties of a multiplier  $M_\varphi: \mathbb{C}[G] \to \mathbb{C}[G]$ 
                  are equivalent.
                  \begin{itemize}
                  \item[{\rm (i)} ] $M_\varphi$ is m.b. from $C^* (G)$ to $C^*_\lambda(G)$,
                  \item[{\rm (ii)} ] $M_\varphi$ is m.b. from $C^* (G)$ to $L(G)$,
                   \item[{\rm (iii)} ] $M_\varphi$ is m.b. from $C^* (G)$ to $C^* (G)$,
                   \item[{\rm (iv)} ] $\varphi \in B(G)$.
                   \end{itemize}
                   Moreover in all cases the m.b. norm is equal to $\|\varphi\|_{B(G)}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that 
                  the natural map $C^*(G) \to L(G)$ (resp. $C^*(G) \to C^*_\lambda(G)$) is a $*$-homomorphism
                  and hence has m.b. norm $=1$. Thus by \eqref{e21} 
                  $\|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to L(G)\|_{mb}\le
                  \|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C^*(G)\|_{mb} 
                   $, and similarly with $C^*_\lambda$ in place of $L$.
                   We claim $  \|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C^*(G)\|_{mb} \le \|\varphi\|_{B(G)}$
                   from which follows
                   $\|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to L(G)\|_{mb}\le \|\varphi\|_{B(G)}$ (and similarly with $C^*_\lambda$ in place of $L$).
                   To prove the claim, assume $\varphi(.)=\langle \xi, \pi(.) \eta\rangle$.
                   Note that 
                   $t\mapsto \pi(t) \otimes \pi_u(t)$ defines a $*$-homomorphism
                    $\nu: C^*(G) \to C_\pi^*(G)\otimes_{\max} C^*(G)$
                   and the linear form $f(T)=\langle \xi, T \eta\rangle$
                   has norm (or m.b. norm) $\le \|\xi\|\|\eta\|$ from $C_\pi^*(G)$ to $\mathbb{C}$. 
                   We have $[M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C^*(G)]= (f\otimes Id) \nu$ and hence 
                   (see \eqref{comp}) $ \|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C^*(G)\|_{mb} \le \|\xi\|\|\eta\|$.
                   Taking the inf over all $\xi,\eta$
                   the claim follows.
                   
                   
                  Conversely 
                  let $x\in \mathbb{C}[G]$. Assume $\|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to L(G)\|_{mb}
                  \le 1 $.
                  We have by universality
                  $$\|x\|_{C^*(G)}=\|\sum x(t) \pi_u(t)\|\ge \|\sum x(t) \pi_u(t)\otimes \rho(t)\|_{C^*(G)\otimes_{\max} C_\rho^*(G)}$$
                  and hence                    $$ \ge  \|\sum x(t) \varphi(t) \lambda(t)\otimes \rho(t)\|_{L(G)\otimes_{\max} C_\rho^*(G)} \ge  \|\sum x(t) \varphi(t) \lambda(t) \rho(t)\|_{B(\ell_2(G))}$$
  and since $\langle \delta_e, \lambda(t) \rho(t) \delta_e\rangle=1$ for all $t$ this is
  $\ge |\sum x(t) \varphi(t)|$, which means
  $$\|x\|_{C^*(G)} \ge |\sum x(t) \varphi(t)|.$$
  This shows $\|\varphi\|_{C^*(G)^*} \le1$, and 
         since $B(G)=C^*(G)^*$ isometrically  $\|\varphi\|_{B(G)} \le1$.  By homogeneity
         we obtain $\|\varphi\|_{B(G)} \le \|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to L(G)\|_{mb}$. 
         By   \eqref{e21},  $\|M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to L(G)\|_{mb}$ is less or equal to the other norms in (i) and (iii).
         The proof is then completed easily.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The inequality $\| M_\varphi: C_\lambda^* (G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)  \|_{mb} \le \|\varphi\|_{B(G)}$ can be proved   using the Fell absorption principle by which
          for any $\pi$ the map $\lambda(t) \mapsto [\lambda \otimes \pi ] (t)$ extends to
          a (faithful) $*$-homomorphism on $C_\lambda^* (G)$. Then using the functional $f(T)=\langle \xi, T \eta\rangle$ and reasoning as above
          we obtain the   inequality in question.\\
                   The converse follows from Theorem \ref{Tmul} and \eqref{comp}
                   since the natural morphism $\pi_1: C^* (G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)$
                   has m.b. norm $=1$, and
                   $[M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)]= [M_\varphi: C_\lambda^* (G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)]\pi_1,$
                   we have $\|\varphi\|_{B(G)} =\|  M_\varphi: C^*(G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)  \|_{mb} \le \| M_\varphi: C_\lambda^* (G) \to C_\lambda^* (G)  \|_{mb}.$

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\Lambda\subset G$ be an arbitrary subset.
                      Let $\varphi: \Lambda \to \mathbb{C}$. 
                      Let $C^*(G)_\Lambda \subset C^*(G)$ 
                      and
                      ${C^*_\lambda(G)}_\Lambda \subset C_\lambda^*(G)$
                       be the corresponding closed subspaces generated by $\Lambda$. 
                      Repeating the preceding argument and 
                      using the Hahn-Banach theorem
                       shows that
                      $$\|M_\varphi : C^*(G)_\Lambda \to L(G)\|_{mb} \le 1
                      \text{  (or equivalently  }   \|M_\varphi : {C^*_\lambda(G)}_\Lambda \to {C^*_\lambda(G)}_\Lambda\|_{mb} \le 1)  $$
                      if and only if $\varphi $ admits an extension
                      $\widetilde \varphi : G \to \mathbb{C}$ with $\| \widetilde \varphi \|_{B(G)}\le 1$.

title: Remark
body_md:
In \cite[Cor. 2.6]{JLM} Junge and Le Merdy prove 
                      that $\|u\|_{dec}=\|u\|_{mb}$  for any {\it finite rank} map
                      $u: A \to B$ between $C^*$-algebras.
                     We will say that a $C^*$-algebra $A$ has the 
                     $c$-MBAP if the identity is the pointwise limit of a net
                     of finite rank maps with m.b. norms at most $c$.
                     By  their characterization of {\it finite rank} maps with 
                     m.b. norm at most $1$ on $A$ (see \cite[Th. 2.1]{JLM}) 
                    this holds if and only if $A$ is nuclear. This extends Lance's classical 
                     theorem that the CPAP  is equivalent to nuclearity.
                  It follows that the MBAP of $C_\lambda^* (G)$ (or of $C ^* (G)$) is equivalent to the amenability of $G$, in sharp contrast to the CBAP.

label: s1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{s1} Let $u: C \to {  N}$ be a unital homomorphism from a $C^*$-algebra $C$ to a von Neumann algebra ${  N}\subset B(H)$.
    Then  $u$ is m.b. if  and only if  $u$ is strongly similar to a $*$-homomorphism, and 
    $$\|u\|_{mb} =\inf\{\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \| \}$$
    where the infimum runs over all invertibles $S \in {  N}$
    such that $S u(.) S^{-1}$ is   a $*$-homomorphism.
head: environment

label: p1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p1}
        Let $u: C \to N  $  be as in Theorem \ref{s1}.        Let $v: N' \to B(H)$ be the inclusion map.
        Then $u$ is strongly similar to a $*$-homomorphism
        if  and only if  the map $v . u : N' \otimes  C\to B(H) $ (defined by
        $v . u (a\otimes b)= v(a)u(b) $ extends to
        a c.b. map $w$ from $N' \otimes_{\max} C$ to $B(H)$.
        Moreover
         \begin{equation}  \label{e9}
         \| w:  N'\otimes_{\max} C \to B(H)\|_{cb} =\inf\{\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \| \}\end{equation}
        where the (attained) inf runs over all invertible  $S\in N$
        such that  $S u(.) S^{-1}$ is   a $*$-homomorphism.\\
        Lastly, if $N'$ admits a cyclic vector in $H$ we have $\|w\|=\|w\|_{cb}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $w$ c.b. Clearly $w$ is still a unital homomorphism,
          and hence if it is c.b. it must be similar to a $*$-homomorphism
          whence the existence of an invertible $S$ on $H$ (with
          $\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \| =\|w\|_{cb} $)
          such that $x\mapsto S w(x) S^{-1} $ is a $*$-homomorphism.
          But restricting this to $N' \otimes 1$ we find that 
          $N' \ni y \mapsto  S y S^{-1}$ is  a $*$-homomorphism. A fortiori
          it is self-adjoint, 
          which implies by a simple calculation 
          ($S y S^{-1}   = (S y^* S^{-1})^* $ and hence $S^*S y=yS^*S$)
          that $|S| \in N''=N$.
          Now $S=U|S|$ with $U$ unitary and the map
          $C\ni x \mapsto  U (|S| u(x) |S|^{-1}) U^{-1}$
          is  a $*$-homomorphism.
          Since $U$ is unitary $C\ni x \mapsto    (|S| u(x) |S|^{-1})  $
           is  a $*$-homomorphism, proving the strong similarity of $u$.
           
           Conversely, if $S\in N$ is such that $C\ni x \mapsto    (S u(x) S^{-1})  $
           is  a $*$-homomorphism denoted by $u_S: C \to N$,
           then obviously $v.u_S $ is a (completely contractive)  
           $*$-homomorphism from $ N'\otimes_{\max} C$ to $B(H)$.
           Then  $a\otimes b \mapsto S^{-1} v.u_S (a\otimes b)   S $
           has cb-norm at most $\|S\|  \| S^{-1}  \|$ on $ N'\otimes_{\max} C$ and since $S$ commutes with $v(b)$, we have
           $S^{-1} v.u_S (a\otimes b)   S = v.u(a\otimes b) $. Thus we 
           conclude that $$\| v.u: N'  \otimes_{\max} C\to B(H)\|_{cb} \le \inf\|S\|  \| S^{-1}  \|.$$
           The converse inequality was proved in the first part. There we also proved that the inf is actually a minimum.\\
             The last assertion follows from  \cite{smith} (see the next remark, already stated in    \cite[Cor. 6.23]{154}).
head: environment

label: cyc
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{cyc} Let $u: E \to N$ be a linear map from
    an operator subspace $E\subset C$ to a von Neumann algebra $N \subset B(H)$.
    Let $\alpha$ be a $C^*$-norm on $N' \otimes_{alg} C $. 
    Assume that  the map $w: N' \otimes_{alg} E \to B(H)$ defined as above by $w(y\otimes x)= y u(x)$ ($y\in N', x\in E$) extends to a bounded map
    on $\overline{N' \otimes_{alg} E}^\alpha$. Then if $N'$ admits a cyclic vector, $w$ is c.b. and
 $$\|w\|_{cb}=\|w\|.$$
    Indeed, since $w$ is an $N'$-bimodule map this follows from
    Roger Smith's result in  \cite{smith}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{e10}
    with $D={N}'$ and $E=C$  
    and by \eqref{e9}  there is $S\in N$ with
   $ \|S\|\| S^{-1}  \|\le \|u\|_{mb}$
    such that $u_S(.)=S u(.) S^{-1}$ is   a $*$-homomorphism into $N$.
    Conversely, since a  $*$-homomorphism has unit mb-norm,
    and left or right multiplication by an element  $x\in N$
    has mb-norm at most $\|x\|$, the fact that
     $u(.)=S^{-1}u_S(.)S$ with   $S\in N$ gives us
    $\|u\|_{mb} \le  \|S\|\| S^{-1}\| $.
head: environment

label: pam
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{pam} Let $A$ be a unital $C^*$-algebra. Let $u: C \to {  N}$ be a unital homomorphism from a  unital operator subalgebra $C\subset A$  to a von Neumann algebra ${  N}\subset B(H)$.
  If $\|u\|_{mb}<\infty$ there is an invertible $S \in {  N}$
  with $\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \|= \|u\|_{mb}   $
       such that $u_S(.)=S u(.) S^{-1}$ is   a  unital   homomorphism with  mb-norm $=1$.
       More precisely, $u$ is strongly similar to a
       homomorphism  with mb-norm $=1$  if and only if it is   m.b. 
      and  we have
         $$\|u\|_{mb} =\inf\{\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \| \mid S\in N \ \ \|u_S\|_{mb}=1\}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $w:  N'\otimes_{\max} C \to B(H)$ be as in the preceding proof, so that by \eqref{e10'}
      $\|w\|_{cb} \le \|w\|_{mb} \le \|u\|_{mb}$. By Paulsen's result
      there is $S\in GL(H)$ such that
      $\|w_S\|_{cb} =1$ with $\|S\| \|S^{-1}\|  \le \|w\|_{cb}$. 
       Restricting to $N'\otimes 1$ as above,
      we see that we may assume $|S|\in N$  and of course
      $w_{|S|}$ is still unital  and completely contractive (c.c.).
      We claim  that $\|u_{|S|}\|_{mb} =1$. 
      Indeed, $w_{|S|}$  extends to a c.c. unital and hence u.c.p. map 
      $\varphi : N'\otimes_{\max} A \to B(H)$ (by the injectivity of $B(H)$).
      This c.p. map $\varphi$
       must be $N'$-bimodular since $N'\otimes 1$ is in its  multiplicative domain (see e.g. \cite[p. 107]{154}). Let $f: A \to B(H)$ be the map
      such that $\varphi(x\otimes a)= x f(a)$ (i.e. $f(a)=\varphi(1\otimes a)$).
      The bimodularity of $\varphi$ implies that $f(a)\in (N')'=N$.
      Since $f: A \to N$ is a u.c.p. map between
      $C^*$-algebras, we have $\|f\|_{mb}=1$ (see Proposition  \ref{L1})
      and  since $f_{|C}=u_{|S|}$  we find $\|u_{|S|}\|_{mb} =1$,
      proving the claim.
       \\ Conversely, if $S\in N$ is invertible such that $\|u_S\|_{mb}= 1$ 
      then as above $\|u\|_{mb} \le \|S\|\| S^{-1}  \| \|u_S\|_{mb}=\|S\|\| S^{-1}  \|$.
      This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $T\in B(H)$  
      and let $N$ 
      be a von Neumann algebra containing $T$.
  The map $\rho_T: {\mathcal{A}} \to N$
      is m.b. if  and only if  there is $S\in N$ invertible  such that $\|STS^{-1}\| \le 1$, and
      $$\| \rho_T\|_{MB({\mathcal{A}},N)}=\inf\{\| S\| \| S^{-1}\|  \}$$
      where the inf (which is attained) runs over all such $S$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The preceding proof actually shows that
      $\|u\|_{mb}=\|w\|_{cb}$, and if $N' \subset B(H)$ is cyclic $\|u\|_{mb}=\|w\|$
      by Remark \ref{cyc}.
head: environment

label: t5.6
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t5.6} Let $M\subset B(H)$ be a von Neumann algebra,
         $\pi: A \to M$   a unital $*$-homomorphism on a (unital) $C^*$-algebra $A $, and
  $\delta: A \to M$   a $\pi$-derivation. 
  Then $\|\delta\|_{mb} <\infty $ if  and only if  there is $\theta \in  M$ such that
  $\delta=\delta^\theta$ and we have
  \begin{equation}\label{chr}
  \|\delta\|_{mb} =2\inf\{ \|T\| \mid T\in  M, \ \delta=\delta^T\} =d(\theta,\pi(A)'), \end{equation}
  where again the infimum is attained.
  Moreover
  $\|\delta\|_{mb}$ coincides with the cb-norm of the 
  mapping $D: M' \otimes_{\max} A \to B(H)$ defined by $D(x\otimes a)=\pi(x)\delta(a)$, and
  $\|\delta\|_{mb}=\| D\|$ if
  $M'$ is cyclic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $\|\delta\|_{mb} <\infty $.
      Then by \eqref{e10} we have
      $\|Id \otimes \delta :  M' \otimes_{\max} A \to M' \otimes_{\max} M\|_{cb} \le \|\delta\|_{mb}$
      and hence $\|D\|_{cb} \le \|\delta\|_{mb}$.
      Let $\Pi: M' \otimes_{\max} A \to B(H)$ be the continuous $*$-homomorphism
      defined by $\Pi(x\otimes a)=x\pi(a) $. It is easy to check that
      $D$ is a $\Pi$-derivation. By Christensen's theorem  
      there is $T\in B(H)$ with $\|T\|= (1/2)\|D\|_{cb}$ such that $D(z)=[\Pi(z), T]$ for any $z\in
      M' \otimes_{\max} A$. 
      Using $z\in M' \otimes 1$ (for which  $D(z)=0$) we find $T\in M''=M$ and using
      $z\in 1 \otimes A$ we find $\delta(a)=[\pi(a),T]$, i.e. $\delta=\delta^T$.
      This proves $2\inf\{\|\theta\| \mid \theta\in M, \delta=\delta^\theta\} \le 2\|T\|= \|D\|_{cb} \le  \|\delta\|_{mb}$.
      Conversely, if $\theta\in M $ and $ \delta=\delta^\theta$ we clearly have $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le 2 \|\theta\|$,
      and hence $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le 2 \inf\{\|\theta\| \mid \theta\in M, \delta=\delta^\theta\}$. 
      This proves  $\|D\|_{cb} =  \|\delta\|_{mb}$
      and the first equality in \eqref{chr}, the second one follows since $\delta^T=\delta^\theta \Leftrightarrow T\in \theta +\pi(A)'$.
      It also proves in passing that $\inf\{\|\theta\| \mid \theta\in M, \delta=\delta^\theta\} $ is attained on $T$.
      The cyclic case follows by Remark \ref{cyc}.
head: environment

label: ptruc
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{ptruc} Assume that $ A \subset M$ and that $\pi$ is the inclusion map.
     Then any m.b. derivation $\delta: A\to M$ extends to an m.b. derivation
     $\widetilde \delta: M \to M$ with  $\|\widetilde \delta\|_{cb} \le  \|\widetilde \delta\|_{mb}=  \|  \delta\|_{mb}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We just set $\widetilde \delta(x)=[x,T]$ with  $T$ attaining the infimum in \eqref{chr}.

label: rcoh
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{rcoh}
The inclusions $M \to L_2(\tau)_c$,
 $M \to L_2(\tau)_r$ and $M \to L_2(\tau)_{oh}$
  are all
 completely contractive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $t=\sum b_j \otimes x_j\in B \otimes M$.
We have  $\|t\|^2_{\min}=\| t^* t\|_{\min}=
\| \sum b_i^* b_j \otimes x_i^* x_j\|_{\min}$, and
since the linear form $x\mapsto \tau(x)$ is completely
contractive from $M$ to $\mathbb{C}$, the latter is
$$\ge \| \sum b_i^* b_j  \tau(x_i^* x_j)\|_B= \| \sum b_i^* b_j  \langle x_i, x_j\rangle\|_B. $$
 This settles the case of $M \to L_2(\tau)_c$. The case of $r$ is similar.
 The case of $oh$ follows by complex interpolation. Indeed, by \cite[p.137]{P4}
 when $B=M_n$ we have $(B\otimes_{\min } H_c, B\otimes_{\min } H_r)_{1/2}= B\otimes_{\min } H_{oh}$. This implies that denoting by
 $j: M \to L_2(\tau)$ the inclusion, the map
  $Id_B \otimes j : B\otimes_{\min } M \to B\otimes_{\min }  L_2(\tau)_{oh}$
  has norm $\le 1$, since it does so for both cases $c$ and $r$.
head: environment

label: RC
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{RC}

Consider the ``diagonal" embedding $x\mapsto (x,x)$ of $H$ into
the o.s. $H_r \oplus H_c$.
We denote by $H_{rc} \subset H_r \oplus H_c$
the o.s. obtained by equipping $H$ with the o.s. structure induced
by $H_r \oplus H_c$ on this diagonal subspace.
For any $t\in B \otimes H$ we have
\begin{equation}\label{e122}\|t\|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{rc}} =\max\{ \|t\|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{r}} ,
\|t\|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{c}} \}. \end{equation}
The space $H_{rc}$ is often (abusively)  denoted $H_r \cap H_c$ to reflect \eqref{e122}.
Similarly, one sets 
$R\cap C=(\ell_2)_{rc}$.
head: environment

label: rcoh1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By classical interpolation theory (see e.g. \cite{BeL}) for any interpolation pair $(A_0 , A_1)$ we have   $\|A_0 \cap A_1\to (A_0 , A_1)_{1/2} \|\le 1$, and hence for any $B$  $$\|(B\otimes_{\min } H_r) \cap (B\otimes_{\min } H_c) \to 
(B\otimes_{\min } H_r, B\otimes_{\min } H_c)_{1/2} \|\le 1.$$
Since    $(B\otimes_{\min } H_r, B\otimes_{\min } H_c)_{1/2}= B\otimes_{\min } H_{oh}$ when $B=M_n$,  the result follows by \eqref{e122}.
head: environment

label: RC1
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{RC1}
Let $(e_j)$ be an orthonormal basis of $H$.
Then for any finitely supported $j\mapsto b_j \in B$
we have
$\|\sum b_j \otimes e_j \|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{r}} =
\|\sum b_j b_j^*\|^{1/2}$,
$\|\sum b_j \otimes e_j \|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{c}} =
\|\sum b^*_j b_j\|^{1/2}$ and
$$\|\sum b_j \otimes e_j \|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{rc}}
= \max\{\|\sum b_j b_j^*\|^{1/2} ,
\|\sum b^*_j b_j\|^{1/2}\}. $$
Moreover
$$\|\sum b_j \otimes e_j \|_{B \otimes_{\min} H_{oh}}
= \|\sum \overline{b_j} \otimes b_j \|_{\overline B \otimes_{\min} B }^{1/2} .$$

label: homo
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{homo} An o.s.  $E$ is called homogeneous if $\|u\|_{cb}=\|u\|$
for any $u: E \to E$. 
The spaces $H_r,H_c,H_{oh}$ and $H_{rc}$ are all examples of homogeneous o.s. 
This implies that   any operator subspace $K\subset H_r$ can be identified with $K_r$ and similarly for $c, oh$ and $rc$.
head: environment

label: rcapc
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rcapc}
         Consider in the direct sum $M_n \oplus M_n$
     the $n$-dimensional subspace $F_n \subset M_n \oplus M_n$ spanned by the family
   $\{e_{1j} \oplus  e_{j1} \}$.  Here we view $M_n \oplus M_n \subset M_{2n}$
   by identifying the elements of $M_n \oplus M_n$ with block diagonal $2n \times 2n$-matrices. This space is often denoted (abusively)  by
         $R_n\cap C_n$   in the context of interpolation between pairs of o.s. It plays an important role in connection
   with free probability questions (see \cite{HP2}).

label: hp2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{hp2}
   For any  $C^*$-algebra $B$ with the WEP we have
         $$C(F_n,B)\ge  (1+\sqrt{n})/2 ,$$
         and equality holds when $B=B(H)$ or $B=M_{2n}$.

label: t3.1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{t3.1}     A von Neumann algebra   $M$
     is injective if and only if  there is $c>0$ such that $C (E_n, M) \ge c \sqrt n$ for all $n$.
head: environment

label: p2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{p2} Let $H=\ell_2$.
           Let $M$ be a finite  von Neumann algebra  with normalized trace $\tau$.
            Let $\alpha: H_{rc} \to M$ be any c.b. map.
            Let $k: M \to L_2(\tau)_{r c}$ be the
            inclusion as in Lemma \ref{rcoh1}.
         Let $T = k\alpha : H_{rc} \to L_2(\tau)_{r  c}$.
         Then 
            \begin{equation}  \label{e16} \forall n\ge 1\quad   a_n(T) C (F_n, M) \le \|T\|_{cb} \le \|\alpha\|_{cb},\end{equation}
            where $$a_n(T)=\inf\{\|T-T'\| \mid rk(T')<n\}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall
                            $\|T\|=a_1(T) \ge \cdots\ge a_n(T)$ and $a_n(T)=\lambda_n(|T|).$
              The polar factorization shows (as is classical) that there is a
              subspace $F\subset H_{rc}$ of dimension $n$  such that  $\|T(x)\| \ge a_n(T) \|x\|$
              for any $x\in F$. We may assume  $  a_n(T)>0$. It follows that
              $\|{T^{-1}}_{|T(F)} \|\le a_n(T)^{-1}$.
              Let $P: L_2(M)_{r  c} \to T(F)$ be the orthogonal projection.
              Note $\|P\|_{cb} \le 1$ and $\|{T^{-1}}_{|T(F)} \|_{cb}=\|{T^{-1}}_{|T(F)} \| $ by homogeneity (see Remark \ref{homo}). We have $Id_F= {T^{-1}}_{|T(F)} P k \alpha_{|F} $ and $\|k\|_{cb}\le 1$ by Lemma \ref{rcoh}.
              Therefore
              $$C(F,M)\le \|{T^{-1}}_{|T(F)} \|_{cb}\|\alpha\|_{cb}   \le a_n(T)^{-1}\|\alpha\|_{cb} .$$
             By homogeneity again,   $F\simeq F_n$ completely isometrically,
             so that $C(F,M)=C(F_n,M)$ and the announced result follows.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Assume  $C (F_n, M) \ge c \sqrt n$ for all $n$. 
                  Then for any $n$ and any $\alpha: H_{rc} \to M$ we have
                  $$\sup \nolimits_n n^{1/2} a_n(k\alpha)   \le c^{-1} \|\alpha\|_{cb}.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To start with we claim that it suffices to prove the theorem in the finite case.
\\ Indeed, if $N\subset M$ is a von Neumann  subalgebra admitting
           a c.c. projection $P: M \to N$ we have obviously
           $$C(F_n, M) \le C(F_n, N).$$
           Therefore the assumption on $M$
           is inherited by $N$, and 
           in particular by $N=pM$ for any central projection $p$ in $M$.
           This shows that the three terms in the decomposition  $M=M_I\oplus M_{II}\oplus M_{III}$ in 
           types I, II (semifinite)  and III all inherit the assumption.
           The type I case is easy since it is always injective.
           Using the subalgebras $pM$ with $p$ finite, 
           which have a weak*-dense directed union, the semifinite case is easily reduced to the finite one.
            Then using  crossed products and Takesaki's
           duality theorem as in \cite[p. 198]{Ha1132} one can treat the type III case.
 This proves our claim that we may assume $M$ finite.

    Assume  $M$ finite and $C (F_n, M) \ge c \sqrt n$ for all $n$. \\
    We will use the traditional notation $OH_n=(\ell_2^n)_{oh}$.
 We have a natural c.c. inclusion
                 $j_n : F_n \to OH_n$
                 (see Lemma \ref{rcoh1}). Let $e_j$ (resp. $t_j$) be an orthonormal basis
                 in $F_n$ (resp. $OH_n$) with (say) $j_n(e_j)= t_j$. Let $y_j\in M$.
                 Consider the map $\gamma_n : OH_n \to M$
                 taking $t_j$ to $y_j$. 
                 Let $\alpha_n= \gamma_nj_n : F_n \to M$ so that $a_n(e_j)= y_j$.
                 We have
                 $$ \| \alpha_n\|_{cb} \le  \| \gamma_n\|_{cb}=  \|\sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j \|_{\min}^{1/2} .$$
     Then \eqref{e16} yields the following:
                     for any $(y_j)$ in $M$ the map $\gamma_n: OH_n \to M$ taking   $(t_j)$ to $(y_j)$
                       satisfies
                       $$\| k \gamma_n \|_{S_{2,\infty} } =\sup\nolimits_m \sqrt m  a_m(k \gamma_n)  \le c'  \|\sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j \|_{\min}^{1/2},$$
                       where $c'=1/c$.       
In other words the map $w_n : \ell_2^n \to L_2(\tau) $
taking $e_j$ to $y_j$ satisfies
 \begin{equation}  \label{e15}
 \| w_n \|_{S_{2,\infty} } \le c' \|\sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j \|_{\min}^{1/2}. \end{equation}
   Since $w_n$ is of rank at most $n$ 
   we have for all $n>1$
   $$\|w_n\|_{S_2}\le \|w_n\|_{S_{2,\infty}} c''\sqrt{\log n}.$$
   Therefore for any $n$-tuple of unitaries $(y_j)$ in $M$
   $$\sqrt n \le c''\sqrt{\log n} \ c' \|\sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j \|_{\min}^{1/2}.$$
   We  then use a well known trick.
   Let $T= \sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j $. Note
   $\|T\|^{2m}=\|(T^*T)^m\|$ and 
   $(T^*T)^m$ when developed is a sum of $n^{2m}$ 
   terms of the form $\bar U\otimes U$ with $U$ unitary in $M$.

   Therefore
   $$ n^m \le (c''c')  \sqrt{\log(n^{2m}) } \|T\|^{m}$$
   and hence
   $$n \le [c''c'  \sqrt{\log(n^{2m}) } ]^{1/m} \|T\|$$
   and letting $m\to \infty$ we obtain
   $$n \le  \|T\|.$$
   This shows that  $\|\sum  \bar{y_j} \otimes y_j \|_{\min} =n$
   for any $n$-tuple of unitaries in $M$ and any $n$.
   This settles the case of factors,
   but since $pM$ satisfies the same assumption
   for any central projection $p\in M$,
   the same conclusion holds holds for $pM$.
   By Haagerup's criterion in \cite[Lemma 2.3]{Ha1132} (due to Connes \cite{Co} for factors), $M$ is injective.
   This proves the ``if part". The converse holds by   \cite[Th. 4.1]{HP2}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The preceding argument is quite similar to one previously used by Marius Junge in \cite{Ju-oh} for the operator Hilbert space $OH_n$ in place of $F_n=R_n\cap C_n$.
 The latter space $OH_n$ (for which we refer to \cite[\S 7]{P4}) is a copy of the $n$-dimension Hilbert space $\ell_2^n$
 sitting  isometrically in $B(H)$ in such a way that
   its orthonormal basis corresponds to elements $t_j\in B(H)$
 such that for any other Hilbert space $K$ and any $a_j \in B(K)$ we have the characteristic identity
 $$\|\sum a_j \otimes t_j \|_{B(K) \otimes_{\min} B(H)} =\|\sum \overline{a_j} \otimes a_j \|^{1/2}_{\overline{B(H)} \otimes_{\min} B(H)}.$$
  In  \cite{Ju-oh}  Junge shows that
 for any WEP $C^*$-algebra $A$ we have $C(OH_n,A)\approx (n/\log(n))^{1/2}$
  except in the very special case when $A=C \otimes_{\min} B$ with
 $C$ commutative and $B$ f.d.  in which case (assuming  $C$ infinite dimensional)
 $C(OH_n,A)\approx n^{1/2}$. Furthermore he shows
 that  $C(OH_n,A)\ge c (n/\log(n))^{1/2}$ for all $n>1$  (for some $c>0$) only if $A$ has the WEP.
 When $A$ is a von Neumann algebra   this yields a characterization of injectivity.
 While our argument for $F_n$ seems somewhat intertwined with Junge's for $OH_n$, we do not see
 either one as a consequence of the other.\\
 The reader will of course have noticed that
 the preceding proof shows that for   $M$ to be injective it
 suffices to have an estimate of the form
 $C(F_n,M) \ge c n^{1/2} (\log(n))^{-\beta}$ for any fixed $\beta>0$.
 Junge made a similar observation for $C(OH_n,A) \ge c n^{1/2} (\log(n))^{-\beta}$  in his characterization of the WEP.

name: The case of $OH_n$

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $H=\ell_2(G)$ ($G=\mathbb{F}_n$ or $G=\mathbb{F}_\infty$)  and let $(\delta_t)_{t\in G} $ be its standard orthonormal basis.
     For any $g\in \{g_j\mid {1\le j\le n}\}$ let $H(g)\subset H$ denote the closed span of
     the family $\{\delta_t\} $ for the (reduced) words $t$ with last letter equal to $g$.
    Since $ \rho(g) (1-P_{H(g)}) = P_{H(g^{-1})} \rho(g)$, one has a decomposition (cf. \cite[p. 896]{HP2})
      $$\rho(g)= \rho(g) P_{H(g)}  + P_{H(g^{-1})}\rho(g). $$
       For a family $(a_j)$ in $B(H)$,  we use the customary notation
     $$|(a_j)|_C=\|\sum a^*_ja_j\|^{1/2} \text{  and  } |(a_j)|_R=\|\sum a_ja^*_j\|^{1/2}.$$
      Let
     $$a_j=\rho(g_j) P_{H(g_j)}  \text{  and  } b_j=P_{H(g_j^{-1})}\rho(g_j) $$
     so that $\rho(g_j)=a_j+b_j$.
 Note that $|(a_j)|_C \le 1$ and $|(b_j)|_R \le 1$. Similarly by \cite{HP2} the same decomposition holds for  $\lambda$ as follows:
  \begin{equation}  \label{e17}
      \lambda(g_j)=\alpha_j +\beta_j \text{  with  }
     |(\alpha_j)|_C \le 1\text{ and }  |(\beta_j)|_R \le 1. \end{equation}

label: e41
title: Remark
body_md:
It is easy to check that
         \begin{equation}  \label{e41} C(E_n,B(H))\ge \sqrt {n}/2 .\end{equation}
         Indeed this boils down to checking that the ``constant of injectivity"
         of $E_n$ is at least $\sqrt {n}/2 $.
          It suffices to  check that if
         $Q: B(H) \to E_n$ is a linear projection, then $\|Q\|_{cb} \ge \sqrt {n}/2 $. 
         We have a decomposition 
         $\lambda(g_j)=\alpha_j+\beta_j$ in $B(H)$  
         whence a decomposition 
         $\lambda(g_j)=Q\alpha_j+Q\beta_j$ in $M_\lambda$.
         Therefore
         $\sqrt n=(\sum\| \lambda(g_j)\|_2)^{1/2}
         \le (\sum\| Q\alpha_j\|_2)^{1/2}
         +(\sum\| Q\beta_j\|_2)^{1/2}
         \le |(Q\alpha_j)|_C +|(Q\beta_j)|_R   
         \le \|Q\|_{cb}  |(\alpha_j)|_C +\|Q\|_{cb}|(\beta_j)|_R\le
         2\|Q\|_{cb} $.\\
         The same argument shows that   $C(E_n,B)\ge \sqrt {n}/2 $ for any $B$ with WEP,
         since in that case the inclusion $B\to B^{**}$ factors through $B(H)$ and $w$ extends to $w^{**}$ on $B^{**}$. \\Note  that since $d_{cb}(E_n,F_n)\le 2$ (see Remark \ref{R3}) we could also derive from Theorem \ref{hp2}
         that $C(E_n,B(H))\ge (1+\sqrt {n})/4$.

label: T10
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T10} Let $c>0$  and $n\ge 1$. Let $G=\mathbb{F}_n$, $H=\ell_2(G)$ and
         let     $A=C^*_\lambda(G)\subset B(H)$.
Let $M$ be a von Neumann algebra such that
         $$\|\delta\|_{mb} \le c \|\delta\|_{cb} $$
         for any derivation $\delta: A \otimes 1_M \to B(H)\bar\otimes M$.
         Then
         \begin{equation}  \label{e32} \sqrt n/2 \le 4 c C(E_n,M).\end{equation}
         Moreover, the same property holds for  $G=\mathbb{F}_\infty$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first claim that there is a derivation
         $D: A \otimes 1 \to B(H)\bar\otimes M_\lambda$ (here for simplicity $1$ denotes the unit
         in $M_\lambda$)
         with $\|D\|_{cb}\le 4$  and such that
         $D(\lambda(g_j) ) = P_e \otimes \lambda(g_j)$
         where $P_e\in B(H)$ is a element of unit norm (namely $P_e$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb{C}\delta_e$) and $g_j$ are the free generators of $G$.
         
         We set for any $x\in A$
         $$D(x\otimes 1)=[x\otimes 1, \Sigma]$$
         with
          $$\Sigma= \sum  - b_j \otimes \alpha_j +a_j \otimes \beta_j .$$
         By a well known operator version of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (see e.g.  \cite[Lemma 2.4]{Ha1132})         we have
         $\|\sum b_j \otimes \alpha_j\|\le \|(b_j)\|_R \|(\alpha_j)\|_C\le 1$ and
         $\|\sum a_j \otimes \beta_j\|\le \|(a_j)\|_C\|(\beta_j)\|_R \le 1$ and hence $\|\Sigma\|\le 2$.
         Therefore $\|D\|_{cb} \le 4$.
         Since $\rho$ and $\lambda$ commute, $\rho(g_j)=a_j+b_j$    commutes with $x\in M_\lambda$ which means $[x,b_j]=-[x,a_j]$ and hence
         \begin{equation}  \label{e30} D(x\otimes 1) =[x\otimes 1, \Delta]\end{equation}
        where
       \begin{equation}  \label{e31} \Delta=   \sum\nolimits_1^n a_j \otimes \lambda(g_j)\in B(H) \otimes E_n  .\end{equation} 
  In particular it is important to observe that for all $x\in A$
  \begin{equation}  \label{e19}
  D(x\otimes 1) \in B(H) \otimes E_n  .
  \end{equation}        
    Let $a_g=\rho(g) P_{H(g)}$. 
     It is easy to check 
  that $[x, a_g]=0$ when $x=\lambda(g')$ with $g'\not=g$
     and $=P_e$  when $x=\lambda(g)$ so that
     $$D(\lambda(g_j)) = P_e \otimes \lambda(g_j) .$$
     This proves the claim.\\
     Consider a factorization of $Id_{E_n}$ through $M$ of the form
  $  E_n {\buildrel {w}\over \rightarrow} M {\buildrel {v}\over \rightarrow}  E_n $.
  
  Let $\delta: A\otimes 1_M \to B(H)\bar\otimes M $ be the derivation defined by
  \begin{equation}  \label{e29}
  \delta(x\otimes 1_M)=[ Id_{B(H)}\otimes w] D(x\otimes 1) =[x\otimes 1_M, [Id_{B(H)}\otimes w](\Delta) ].\end{equation}
  By our assumption
   $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le c\|\delta\|_{cb}\le c\|w\|_{cb} \|D\|_{cb}\le 4c\|w\|_{cb}.$ 
  
  By Corollary \ref{ptruc} our derivation
  $\delta$ admits an extension $\hat \delta: B(H) \otimes 1_M \to B(H)\bar \otimes M$ with
 $$\|\hat \delta\|_{cb} \le \|\delta\|_{mb} \le 4c \|w\|_{cb}.$$
 Then    $\hat\delta(\lambda(g_j) \otimes 1_M)=\delta(\lambda(g_j) \otimes 1_M)=P_e \otimes w(   \lambda(g_j))$, and hence $\hat\delta(x \otimes 1_M) =P_e \otimes w(  x)$ for all $x\in E_n$.
 Let $f\in B(H)^*$ be of unit norm such that $f(P_e)=1$.
  We may view the map $f\otimes v$
  as one from ${B(H) \bar\otimes M }$ to ${E_n }$ with c.b. norm $\le \|v\|_{cb}$
  since obviously $\|f: B(H) \to \mathbb{C}\|_{cb}=1$.
 Let $w': E_n \to B(H)$  and  $v': B(H) \to E_n$ be defined by $w'(x)= x\otimes 1_M$
 and let $v'(b) = [f  \otimes   v    ]\hat \delta(b\otimes 1) $. 
 Then $v'w'(x) =vw(x)$ for all $x\in E_n$. 
 Thus $v'w' =Id_{E_n}$ is a factorization through $B(H)$ and hence if $c=\|  \delta\|_{mb}  \|\delta\|^{-1}_{cb}$
 $$C(E_n,B(H))\le \|v'\|_{cb} \|w'\|_{cb} \le \|v\|_{cb} \|\hat \delta\|_{cb} 
  \le \|v\|_{cb} \|  \delta\|_{mb} =  c \|v\|_{cb}  \|\delta\|_{cb}  \le 4c \|v\|_{cb}\|w\|_{cb}.$$
 Taking the infimum over $v,w$ we obtain
 $$C(E_n,B(H))\le 4c C(E_n,M),$$
   and we conclude by \eqref{e41}.
 
   
 Lastly, assume now that $G=\mathbb{F}_\infty$.  
  Let $(g_j)$ denote the free generators of $\mathbb{F}_\infty$. 
 Then \eqref{e29}, \eqref{e30} and \eqref{e31}  can still be used to define the desired derivation, using for
 $(g_1,\cdots,g_n)$ the first free generators of $\mathbb{F}_\infty$.

label: exa
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{exa} 
      Let $G=\mathbb{F}_\infty$, $A=C^*_\lambda(G)$ and  $H=\ell_2(G)$.
      Assume that
      all c.b. derivations from $A\otimes 1_M$ to $B(H)\bar \otimes M $ are m.b.
      Then
       there is $c'>0$ such that $C(E_n,M)\ge c' \sqrt n$ for all $n\ge 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the closed graph theorem, if the (closed) subspaces 
   of derivations in $MB(A,B(H)\bar \otimes M)$ and
   $CB(A,B(H)\bar \otimes M)$ coincide, they must have equivalent norms, and then
    the corollary follows from \eqref{e32}  by the last assertion of  Theorem \ref{T10}.
head: environment

label: exa1
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{exa1} 
      Let $G=\mathbb{F}_\infty$, $A=C^*_\lambda(G)$ and  $M_\lambda=C^*_\lambda(G)''$.          There is a c.b. derivation  from $ A\otimes 1 $ to $ B(H)\bar \otimes M_\lambda$ that is not m.b.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
By Remark \ref{R2}, if $Q(x\otimes 1)=q(x)\otimes 1$, we have
    $\| D Q\|_{mb}=\|D\|_{mb}$ for any map $D$ defined on $A\otimes 1$.
      Therefore we also obtain
       a similar example of a derivation from
      $\mathscr{C}\otimes 1\simeq\mathscr{C}$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $N=M_2(B(H)\bar \otimes M_\lambda)$.
There is a c.b. unital homomorphism $u: \mathscr{C} \to N$ that does not admit any c.b. lifting $\hat u: \mathscr{C} \to W$ when $W$ is any WEP
$C^*$-algebra of which  $N$ is a quotient.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $W$ is WEP we have
$\|\hat u\|_{mb} =\|\hat u\|_{cb}$ for any   $\hat u\in CB( \mathscr{C} , W)$.
Let $q: W \to N$ be a quotient map so that $u=q\hat u$.
Then $\|u\|_{mb} \le \|q\|_{mb} \|\hat u\|_{mb} \le \|\hat u\|_{cb}$.
When $u$ is associated to a derivation $\delta: \mathscr{C} \to B(H)\bar \otimes M$ as in \eqref{e18}, 
we have clearly $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le \|u\|_{mb}$, so
this gives us $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le \|\hat u\|_{cb}$.
Taking Remark \ref{R2} into account, we can select a $u$ associated to a  c.b. $\delta$
with $\|\delta\|_{mb}=\infty$ and 
 the corollary follows.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Actually the preceding argument shows that
           in the case $n=\infty$ there is no $c<\infty$ for which the homomorphism $u$
           is   locally $c$-liftable  in the sense of \cite[Def. 7.46]{154}.

title: Remark
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote the full Fock space based
         on a Hilbert space with orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ ($1\le j\le n$).
         Consider in $B(\mathcal{F})$ the left (resp. right) creation operator $\ell_j$ (resp. $r_j$)
         taking $x\in \mathcal{F}$ to $e_j \otimes x$ (resp. $  x\otimes e_j$). Let $\Omega$ denote the vacuum vector. Let $s_j=\ell_j+\ell_j^*$ and $t_j=r_j + r_j^*$.
         In Voiculescu's free probability theory \cite{VDN}, the families $(s_j)$ and $(t_j)$ are mutually commuting and each of them is a free gaussian (or semicircular) family with respect to the state
         $f_\Omega: x\mapsto \langle \Omega, x\Omega \rangle$.
         Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the $C^*$-algebra generated by $(s_j)$ in $B(\mathcal{F})$ and let $\mathcal{M}$
         denote the von Neumann algebra generated by $\mathcal{A}$. Note that $\mathcal{M}' =\mathcal{A}'$ is generated by $(t_j)$.
         When restricted to $\mathcal{M}$ or to $\mathcal{M}'  $, the state  $f_\Omega$ defines a normalized trace
         that we denote by $\tau$.
         Let $\mathcal{E}_n$ denote the linear span of $(s_j)_{1\le j\le n}$ viewed as an operator subspace of
         $\mathcal{M}$.
         It is  known that the orthogonal projection from $L_2(\tau)$ onto $\mathcal{E}_n$
         defines a projection $Q: \mathcal{M}\to \mathcal{E}_n$ with $\|Q\|_{cb} \le 2$.
         Let $P=Q_{|\mathcal{A}}:\mathcal{A} \to  \mathcal{M}  $.
          In complete analogy with
         Theorem \ref{T10} we can produce a derivation
         \def{\mathcal{D}}{{\mathcal{D}}}
         $\mathcal{D}: \mathcal{A} \otimes 1 \to B(\mathcal{F}) \bar \otimes \mathcal{M}$
          such that $x\mapsto [f_\Omega \otimes Q] {\mathcal{D}} (x \otimes 1)$ is
         equal to $P(x)$ for all $x\in \mathcal{A}$. 
         One simply sets
         $${\mathcal{D}}(a\otimes 1)=\sum [a,r_j] \otimes s_j .$$
          As for Theorem \ref{T10} we can check that $\|\mathcal{D}\|_{cb} \le 4$ and $\sqrt n \le 2\|{\mathcal{D}}\|_{mb}$.

name: Free gaussian analogue

label: R3
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{R3}
By Haagerup's by now classical results in \cite{Ha}
   the map $w: F_{n} \to E_n$ defined by 
   $w([e_{1j}\oplus e_{j1}])=\lambda(g_j)$ has $\|w\|_{cb} \le 2$ and the inverse map
   $w^{-1}$ admits an extension $v: M_\lambda \to  F_{n}$ with
   $\|v\|_{cb}\le 1$. In particular $d_{cb}(E_n,F_n)\le 2$, and also $d_{cb}(\mathcal{E}_n,F_n)\le 2$.  \\
   The proof that $\|w\|_{cb} \le 2$ can be derived easily from the decomposition \eqref{e17} : setting 
   $ w=w_1+w_2$ with $w_1([e_{1j}\oplus e_{j1}]) = a_j$ and $w_2([e_{1j}\oplus e_{j1}]) =b_j $
   we obtain c.c. maps $w_1,w_2$ from $F_n$ to $B(H)$ such that
   $ w=w_1+w_2$ on $F_n$. 
   As for $v: M_\lambda \to  F_{n}$, we use Remark \ref{homo}:
   denoting by $k:  M_\lambda \to L_2(M_\lambda, \tau)_{rc}$
   the inclusion in Lemma \ref{rcoh1} the o.s. $F_n$ can be identified completely isometrically with the operator subspace
   $F=k(E_n)\subset L_2(M_\lambda, \tau)_{rc}$, and the
   orthogonal projection $P_F$ on $L_2(M_\lambda, \tau)_{rc}$   has $\|P_F\|_{cb}\le 1$.
   Thus we can take for 
   $v$ the inclusion $k: M_\lambda \to L_2(M_\lambda, \tau)_{rc}$ 
   followed by   $P_F$.   
      In particular this implies
  \begin{equation}  \label{e27} C(F_{n}, M_\lambda)\le 2.\end{equation}

label: pinj
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{pinj} Let  $N$ be an   injective von Neumann algebra.   
          \\ For any unital $C^*$-algebra $A$
          any unital c.b. homomorphism $u$  from $A$  to $N$  
          is strongly similar
          to a $*$-homomorphism, and  we have $\|u\|_{mb}=\|u\|_{cb}$.\\
           Moreover, any c.b. derivation $\delta: A\to M$ relative to a $*$-homomorphism $\pi:A\to M$
          is inner and $\|\delta\|_{mb}=\|\delta\|_{cb}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since injective von Neumann algebras have the WEP, the equality $\|u\|_{mb}=\|u\|_{cb}$
           follows from (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) in Theorem
           \ref{wep}.
                      Strong similarity follows by Theorem \ref{s1}.\\
          Assume $M\subset B(H)$. Consider a c.b. derivation $\delta:A \to M$ relative to $\pi$.
        Viewing it as  $B(H)$-valued we find $\|\delta\|_{cb}=2\min\{\|T\| \mid T\in B(H) \ \delta=\delta^T\}$.
        Let $P: B(H) \to M$ be a conditional expectation projecting $B(H)$ onto $M$.
        Note $\delta=\delta^T$ implies $\delta=\delta^{P(T)}$, with  $P(T)\in M$  and $\|P(T)\|\le \|T\|$. Therefore
        by \eqref{chr}  $\|\delta\|_{mb} \le \|\delta\|_{cb}$ and the rest  is clear.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
In the terminology of c.b. Hochschild cohomology presented in \cite{SS}
          the last assertion in Prop. \ref{pinj} means that
          $H^1_{cb}(\pi(A),M)=\{0\}$ for any $\pi$, or simply $H^1_{cb}(A,M)=\{0\}$ for any unital 
          $C^*$-subalgebra $A\subset M$.
head: environment

label: T55
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{T55} 
     A von Neumann algebra
  ${\cal M}$  is injective if and only if
     all c.b. homomorphisms 
    with range $B(\ell_2) \bar\otimes {\cal M}$ are strongly similar to a $*$-homomorphism
    (or equivalently are m.b.).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H=\ell_2$. 
           Assume all  c.b. homomorphisms 
    with range $B(H) \bar\otimes {\cal M}$ are m.b. This assumption on $B(H) \bar\otimes {\cal M}$ obviously passes to $M_2(B(H) \bar\otimes {\cal M})$.
     It follows (see  \eqref{e18})
     that all c.b. derivations with range in $B(H) \bar\otimes {\cal M}$ are m.b.  which implies
     by an elementary argument that the c.b. and m.b. norms must be equivalent
     on the space of derivations considered in Theorem \ref{T55}.
     Then  ${\cal M}$ is injective by Corollary \ref{exa} and Theorem \ref{t3.1}. \\
     Conversely, if  ${\cal M}$ is injective
     so is $N=B(H) \bar\otimes {\cal M}$ 
     so the converse holds by Proposition \ref{pinj}.
head: environment

label: cfin
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{cfin}  Let $M$ a von Neumann algebra. The following are equivalent:
       \begin{itemize}     \item[{\rm (i)} ] Any c.b. unital homomorphism into $M$ is strongly similar to a $*$-homomorphism.
           \item[{\rm (ii)}] Any c.b. unital homomorphism into $M$ is m.b.
        \item[{\rm (iii)}] $M$ can be decomposed as $M=M_1\oplus M_2$ with $M_1$ injective and $M_2$ finite.
        \item[{\rm (iv)}] Any c.b. derivation $\delta: A\to M$ relative to a unital $*$-homomorphism $\pi:A\to M$
        (on any unital $C^*$-algebra $A$)
          is m.b.
            \item[{\rm (v)}] Any c.b. derivation $\delta: A\to M$ relative to a $*$-homomorphism $\pi:A\to M$
             (on any unital $C^*$-algebra $A$)
          is inner.\\ Equivalently, $H^1_{cb}(A, M)=\{0\}$ for any unital $C^*$-subalgebra $A\subset M$.
              \end{itemize}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first two assertions are equivalent by Theorem \ref{s1}.
 Assume (i). By the structure theory of von Neumann algebras (see e.g. \cite[III.1.4.1]{bla} and  \cite[III.1.5.6]{bla}), we have a decomposition 
 of the form $M=M_1\oplus M_2$ with $M_2$ finite and $M_1$ properly infinite, which implies $M_1=B(\ell_2)\bar\otimes M_1$. 
 Clearly each of    $M_1, M_2$ inherits the  property (i).
 By Theorem \ref{T55} $M_1$ is injective, which gives us (iii).
 Assume (iii). Then $M_1$ satisfies (i) by Proposition \ref{pinj} and $M_2$ does by Vasilescu and Zsid\'o's
 result in \cite{VZ}. Then (i) follows. Thus (i), (ii) and (iii) are equivalent.\\
 We already know (iv) $\Leftrightarrow$ (v) by Theorem \ref{t5.6}. Clearly $M$ satisfies (iii) $\Leftrightarrow$ $M_2(M)$ satisfies (iii) $\Leftrightarrow$ $M_2(M)$ satisfies (ii) and the latter implies that $M$ satisfies  (iv) (see \eqref{e18}). This shows (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv). Assume (iv).
 Note that for any decomposition $M=M_1\oplus M_2$
 the inclusion $M_1\subset M$ is max-isometric, so that $M_1$ inherits (iv) from $M$.
  Let $M_1=B(\ell_2)\bar\otimes N$ be the properly infinite part  of $M$.
  By Corollary \ref{exa} and Theorem \ref{t3.1}
  $N$ and hence $M$ must be injective, which means that (iii) holds. Thus (iv) $\Leftrightarrow$ (iii).
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
It is erroneously claimed in \cite{fang} (using \cite[Lemma 2.3]{[19]}) that all QWEP von Neumann algebras satisfy
(i) in Theorem \ref{cfin}.
